title: Pointer arithmetic and valid traversal boundaries
learningObjectives: Apply pointer addition and subtraction only within one array object and its one-past position.
Explain why pointer arithmetic advances by elements rather than raw bytes.
Use pointer comparisons to traverse a valid array range.
Explain when pointer subtraction is defined and its ptrdiff_t result.
Avoid dereferencing one-past pointers or comparing unrelated pointers relationally.

understand.concept: Pointer arithmetic is defined within an array object and one position past its final element. Adding one to a pointer advances by one element of the pointed-to type, not one byte. A one-past pointer may be used as an end marker but must not be dereferenced. Subtracting two pointers is defined when both point into the same array object or one past it, and the result has type ptrdiff_t.
understand.whyItMatters: This knowledge helps reason about C data representation, object bounds and valid memory access.
understand.analogy: Think of memory objects as labelled storage and pointers as typed references to that storage.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal pointer, lifetime and object-access rules.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Pointer addition

If p points to an element of an array, `p + 1` points to the next element, scaled by the size of the pointed-to type. Pointer arithmetic is not general integer arithmetic and must remain within the same array object or its one-past position.

## 2. One-past end pointer

For an array of N elements, `array + N` is a valid one-past pointer. It can be compared with another pointer in the same array range and used as an iteration endpoint. It does not designate an element and must not be dereferenced.

## 3. Pointer subtraction

Subtracting two pointers into the same array object, including its one-past position, produces the number of elements between them. The result type is ptrdiff_t, declared in `<stddef.h>`. The difference must be representable in ptrdiff_t.

## 4. Comparisons

Equality comparisons can be used for compatible pointer values. Relational comparisons such as < and > have defined array-order meaning when the pointers refer to elements of the same array object or its one-past position. Do not use relational comparisons to order unrelated objects.

## 5. Prefer range-based traversal

Use a begin pointer and an end pointer for a range. Ensure both refer to the same array object, and stop before dereferencing end. This pattern makes the boundary visible and avoids computing an invalid index.

questions.prompt: What does p + 1 do when p points to an element of an int array?
options: Advances to the next int element
questions.answer: Advances to the next int element
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type.

questions.prompt: May a one-past pointer be dereferenced?
options: Yes, it refers to an extra element
Only when the array is global
questions.explanation: A one-past pointer is an allowed endpoint, not an accessible element.

options: When both pointers refer into the same array object or its one-past position
For any two pointer values in the program
Only when both pointers are null
questions.answer: When both pointers refer into the same array object or its one-past position
questions.explanation: C defines pointer subtraction for positions within the same array object.

questions.prompt: What type represents a pointer difference?
questions.explanation: The subtraction result has type ptrdiff_t.

questions.prompt: Should relational pointer comparisons be used to order unrelated objects?
options: Yes, their numeric addresses always define portable order
questions.explanation: Relational pointer ordering is only defined for positions within the same array object.
